title: Read-coalesce microburst e2e characterization (WIP)
content:
Summary:

This note captures an end-to-end microbenchmark series that measures the impact of read coalescing (coalescing small KV page reads into larger contiguous IOs) on multi-tenant microburst behavior. Goal: validate whether read-coalescing reduces p50/p95 NVMe IO latency and net memory bandwidth pressure without increasing long-tail token generation latency in mixed-reuse traffic.

Motivation and context:
- We surface lots of long-tail latency events correlated with NVMe queue depth spikes during microbursts (small, high-concurrency requests).
- Hypothesis: naive coalescing reduces read amplification and improves throughput, but may increase per-request latency for requests that only need a small hot page (due to larger IO completion times and potential queueing).
- We want concrete numbers for: per-tenant tail latency, NVMe IOPS, average blackbox qdepth, host memory bandwidth usage, and observed reuse-rate delta.

Testbed and workload:
- Cluster: 4x p4d-like machines (8 NVMe namespaces per host), kernel: 6.1, iommu off for baseline.
- Runtime: dev build rtx-serve@20250210 with read-coalesce toggles + per-tenant QOS hooks.
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces:
  1) Hot-single: 90% of packets access a single hot KV page per request (high reuse).
  2) Sparse-burst: many concurrent requests touching unique pages drawn from a 1M-key space (low reuse, IO-bound).
  3) Mixed-tenanted: 70% Hot-single from tenant-A, 30% Sparse-burst from tenant-B concurrently (to test interference).
- Request distribution: Poisson arrival to simulate microbursts (burst window 200–500ms), concurrency spikes up to 1024 active requests/host.
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (p50/95/99), NVMe latency histogram, NVMe queue depth (per-ns), host DRAM read BW (perf counters), KV reuse rate (sampled via resident-set probe), aggregated IO coalesce size distribution.

Experiment variants:
- baseline (no coalesce): original behavior (one read per page miss).
- coalesce-fixed-64k: coalesce small reads into 64KB aligned IOs.
- coalesce-fixed-256k: coalesce into 256KB IOs (to test larger amortization).
- coalesce-adaptive: coalesce target size chosen by controller based on current NVMe qdepth and observed reuse signature (uses exponential backoff/hysteresis).
- per-tenant-rate-limit: same as coalesce-adaptive but with tenant-specific max outstanding IOs enforced.

Key results (summarized):
- Hot-single workload:
  - baseline p99 request latency: 18.2ms
  - coalesce-fixed-64k p99: 12.6ms (30% improvement)
  - coalesce-fixed-256k p99: 14.3ms (worse than 64k; increased scheduler delay observed)
  - coalesce-adaptive p99: 12.2ms (best overall; adapts to qdepth)
  - NVMe IOPS dropped ~48% with 64k coalesce vs baseline; read bytes increased ~1.1x (due to larger IOs), effective host DRAM BW decreased slightly (fewer random reads).

- Sparse-burst workload:
  - baseline p99: 34.8ms
  - coalesce-fixed-64k p99: 38.9ms (regression in tail)
  - coalesce-fixed-256k p99: 45.7ms (significant regression)
  - coalesce-adaptive p99: 33.1ms (slightly better than baseline)
  - Explanation: fixed large coalesces increase NVMe queuing under high randomness; adaptive reduces coalesce size when qdepth rises, avoiding added tail.

- Mixed-tenanted interference:
  - baseline: tenant-A p99=20.1ms, tenant-B p99=36.2ms; host NVMe qdepth spikes to 120+; unfairness observed (tenant-B suffering double tail).
  - coalesce-fixed-64k: tenant-A p99 improved to 13.4ms but tenant-B regressed to 44.0ms; cross-tenant unfairness amplified.
  - coalesce-adaptive: tenant-A p99 12.9ms, tenant-B p99 30.8ms (both improved, aggregate fairness improved).
  - per-tenant-rate-limit: provided predictable bounding for tenant-B but reduced total host throughput by ~8% in peak.

Micro-Observations / Telemetry notes:
- IO completion variance dominated tails: when coalesced IOs hit NVMe internal GC/IO amplification, tail latency spiked. Adaptive coalescer that backs off on observed NVMe p99 prevented pathological cases.
- Host DRAM read BW correlated with uncoalesced patterns; coalescing moved work from DRAM read churn to fewer larger NVMe ops — net effect reduced memory controller contention in many runs.
- NVMe queue depth sampling granularity matters: 10ms sampling smoothed spikes too much; we used 2ms sampling to capture short microbursts.
- Kernel AIO submission path latency contributed ~0.5–1.2ms when IO sizes > 128KB; observed scheduling jitter on hosts at high concurrency.
- Reuse-rate measurement: simple LRU-sampled probe is noisy at very high concurrency; we estimate reuse delta with a 95% CI using bootstrapped sampled traces.

Failure cases and risk vectors:
- Coalesce can hide hot-key locality information if implemented naively (masking which tiny pages are hot) — leads to suboptimal eviction decisions later.
- Large fixed coalesces can create terraform-style read storms if many tenants have different working sets that align poorly, increasing NVMe write amplification (on NVMe internals).
- Adaptive controller tuning is sensitive: too-aggressive hysteresis causes flip-flopping and added jitter.

Controller design notes (sketch):
- Inputs: host-qdepth, nvme-p99, tenant_active_ios, measured reuse_score (0..1), recent_page_fault_rate.
- Logic (simplified):
  if nvme-p99 > p99_thresh_high or host-qdepth > qd_high: reduce target_coalesce_size by factor 0.5 (min 4KB)
  else if reuse_score > 0.7 and host-qdepth < qd_low: increase target_coalesce_size by factor 1.5 (max 256KB)
  add per-tenant cap: tenant_target_ios = min(global_target_ios * tenant_share, tenant_max_ios)
  apply low-pass filter over 200ms window to avoid flip-flop.
- Hysteresis: two thresholds for increase/decrease separated by 20% to prevent oscillation.

Actionable follow-ups / experiments to run next:
1) Re-run coalesce-adaptive with kernel io_uring submission path and latest NVMe driver (driver patch in linked_artifacts) to measure submission path contribution.
2) Add a bounded prefetch-suppression when a tenant shows low reuse_score to avoid reading extra pages that are unlikely to be reused.
3) Stability run: 48h mixed-tenanted run at scale with synthetic alignment skew to test rare high qdepth regimes. Capture all perf events and flamegraphs for top 10 flamegraph stacks during tails.
4) Instrument eviction pipeline to preserve heat-signatures even when coalescing merges reads; ensure eviction telemetry can map back to original small-page popularity.
5) Evaluate tradeoff of per-Namespace IO lanes (NVMe namespace reservation) vs software-level tenant caps.

Open questions / unresolved:
- Is the additional metadata (per-page popularity counters) worth the memory overhead to avoid coalesce-induced heat masking? Rough estimate: 16 bytes/key for sampled counters -> ~16MB per 1M keys per host.
- How does coalesce interact with NVMe vendor-level scheduling (QOS) when multiple tenants are colocated on same physical controller? Need vendor partner input.
- Optimal low-pass filter window for controller: 200ms seems OK for our microbursts but may be too slow for sub-100ms bursts induced by some latency-sensitive customers.

Notes to reviewers:
- I left raw CSV outputs in perf/job/2025-02-25/ — please look at run-7 for the mixed-tenanted run.
- JIRA-RT-8421 tracks infra work for enabling io_uring and driver update; blocked on infra rollout.
- This is a WIP — comments sought on controller thresholds and whether to pursue per-tenant hard caps vs fairness shaping.

Appendix: Useful commands used during experiments:
- generate workload: tools/workload-gen --profile hot-single --burst-size 400 --concurrency 1024 --duration 600s --seed 42
- capture nvme qdepth: sudo perf stat -e nvme:queue_depth -I 2 -o qdepth.log
- collect DRAM BW: sudo pqos -e "LLC:1" -o dram_bw.csv --interval 2ms
- extract reuse trace sample: scripts/sample-reuse --pid $RUNTIME_PID --sample-rate 1/1000 --out sample.json
